title: If you only have a single class A, how can you prove it follows OOP principles (encapsulation, abstraction, polymorphism via overloading, inheritance via Object)?
shortTitle: How can a single class prove it follows OOP principles?

s1_definition.profdef: Even a SINGLE class with NO explicit extends, NO interfaces, and NO sibling classes demonstrates ALL four OOP pillars. ENCAPSULATION: private fields + public methods control access to internal state. ABSTRACTION: the class exposes public methods (WHAT it does) while hiding private helper methods and internal logic (HOW it does it). POLYMORPHISM: method overloading within the SAME class — multiple methods with the same name but different parameter types (`deposit(BigDecimal amount)` and `deposit(BigDecimal amount, String narration)`) — this is compile-time polymorphism. INHERITANCE: every Java class implicitly extends `java.lang.Object`, inheriting `toString()`, `equals()`, `hashCode()`, `getClass()`, `clone()`, `wait()`, `notify()`, `finalize()`. You can OVERRIDE these inherited methods — proving runtime polymorphism even in a single class.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the bank has ONLY one type of account — just "Account." No SavingsAccount, no CurrentAccount. Can this single Account class still be object-oriented? YES! Encapsulation: balance is private, only deposit/withdraw can change it. Abstraction: `deposit(amount)` hides the 5 internal steps (validate, update balance, log, notify, audit). Polymorphism: `deposit(1000)` and `deposit(1000, "Salary credit")` — same name, different parameters (overloading). Inheritance: Account implicitly extends Object — you override `toString()` to print "SAV2001: Rs.125000" instead of "com.bank.Account@1a2b3c".
s1_definition.oneliner: Single class = encapsulation (private fields), abstraction (public methods hide internal logic), polymorphism (method overloading), inheritance (implicitly extends Object → override toString/equals/hashCode). ALL FOUR PILLARS in ONE class.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Even a SINGLE class with NO explicit extends, NO interfaces, and NO sibling classes demonstrates ALL four OOP pillars. ENCAPSULATION: private fields + public methods control access to internal state. ABSTRACTION: the class exposes public methods (WHAT it does) while hiding private helper methods and internal logic (HOW it does it). POLYMORPHISM: method overloading within the SAME class — multiple methods with the same name but different parameter types (`deposit(BigDecimal amount)` and `deposit(BigDecimal amount, String narration)`) — this is compile-time polymorphism. INHERITANCE: every Java class implicitly extends `java.lang.Object`, inheriting `toString()`, `equals()`, `hashCode()`, `getClass()`, `clone()`, `wait()`, `notify()`, `finalize()`. You can OVERRIDE these inherited methods — proving runtime polymorphism even in a single class.

This is a TRICKY interview question designed to test whether you truly understand OOP principles or just memorize "parent-child class" examples. The answer proves that OOP is embedded in the LANGUAGE itself — not just a design pattern you apply.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the bank has ONLY one type of account — just "Account." No SavingsAccount, no CurrentAccount. Can this single Account class still be object-oriented? YES! Encapsulation: balance is private, only deposit/withdraw can change it. Abstraction: `deposit(amount)` hides the 5 internal steps (validate, update balance, log, notify, audit). Polymorphism: `deposit(1000)` and `deposit(1000, "Salary credit")` — same name, different parameters (overloading). Inheritance: Account implicitly extends Object — you override `toString()` to print "SAV2001: Rs.125000" instead of "com.bank.Account@1a2b3c".

**One line to remember:** Single class = encapsulation (private fields), abstraction (public methods hide internal logic), polymorphism (method overloading), inheritance (implicitly extends Object → override toString/equals/hashCode). ALL FOUR PILLARS in ONE class.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — An interviewer asks: "Show me ALL four OOP pillars using ONLY one class — no interfaces, no inheritance hierarchy, no parent-child."** The developer creates a single `BankAccount` class that proves: (1) encapsulation — private balance + controlled deposit/withdraw, (2) abstraction — public deposit hides 4 private steps, (3) polymorphism — three overloaded deposit methods + override toString/equals/hashCode from Object, (4) inheritance — implicitly extends Object, inherits and overrides its methods. The test class demonstrates each pillar independently with assertions.

**What the project will show:** ONE class proving ALL four pillars, private fields (encapsulation), private helper methods (abstraction), method overloading (compile-time polymorphism), Object inheritance + toString/equals/hashCode override (runtime polymorphism), and a test that verifies each pillar.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1 — ENCAPSULATION.** `new BankAccount("SAV2001", "Rajesh", 125000)` creates the account. balance is private. `account.balance = 0` does NOT compile. Only `deposit()` and `withdraw()` can change the balance — and they VALIDATE before changing.

**Step 2 — ABSTRACTION.** `account.deposit(5000)` looks like ONE simple step. Internally: `validatePositive(5000)` → `updateBalance(5000)` → `logTransaction("CREDIT", 5000, "")`. Three private methods execute. The caller sees NONE of this. Tomorrow, if we add a fourth step (send SMS), the caller's code doesn't change.

**Step 3 — POLYMORPHISM (compile-time).** `deposit(5000)`, `deposit(85000, "Salary")`, `deposit(1000, "Gift", "NEFT-UTR-ABC123")` — THREE different method signatures, ONE method name. The compiler picks the correct version based on arguments. This IS polymorphism — "many forms" of the same deposit method.

**Step 4 — INHERITANCE + POLYMORPHISM (runtime).** BankAccount implicitly extends Object. `toString()` is overridden: `account.toString()` returns "SAV2001 (Rajesh): Rs.216000.50" instead of "BankAccount@1a2b3c". `Object ref = account; ref.toString();` — the JVM dispatches to BankAccount.toString() at RUNTIME, not Object.toString(). This IS runtime polymorphism via inheritance.

**Step 5 — PROOF.** `assertThat(account).isInstanceOf(Object.class)` — BankAccount IS-A Object (inheritance). HashSet treats two accounts with same accountId as equal (equals + hashCode overridden from Object). All four pillars in ONE class, ZERO interfaces, ZERO explicit extends.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ SINGLE CLASS — ALL FOUR PILLARS ═══

  class BankAccount /* extends Object */ {

      ENCAPSULATION:
      ├─ private balance              ← cannot access directly
      ├─ public deposit(amount)       ← controlled modification
      └─ public getBalance()          ← controlled read (no setBalance!)

      ABSTRACTION:
      ├─ public deposit(amount)       ← WHAT (caller sees)
      ├─ private validatePositive()   ← HOW (hidden)
      ├─ private updateBalance()      ← HOW (hidden)
      └─ private logTransaction()     ← HOW (hidden)

      POLYMORPHISM (compile-time — overloading):
      ├─ deposit(BigDecimal amount)
      ├─ deposit(BigDecimal amount, String narration)
      └─ deposit(BigDecimal amount, String narration, String ref)
      Same name, different parameters → compiler picks at compile time

      INHERITANCE (from Object) + POLYMORPHISM (runtime):
      ├─ @Override toString()    ← inherited from Object, overridden
      ├─ @Override equals()      ← inherited from Object, overridden
      └─ @Override hashCode()    ← inherited from Object, overridden
      Object ref = bankAccount;
      ref.toString() → calls BankAccount.toString() at RUNTIME!
  }

  ZERO explicit extends. ZERO interfaces. ZERO sibling classes.
  ALL FOUR PILLARS PRESENT. (Recommended) 
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Even a single class with no explicit extends or implements demonstrates all four OOP pillars. Encapsulation: private fields like balance can only be changed through public methods like deposit and withdraw that validate every modification — there is no setBalance method. Abstraction: the public deposit method hides three private steps (validatePositive, updateBalance, logTransaction) — the caller knows WHAT happens (deposit money) but not HOW it happens internally. Polymorphism has TWO forms in a single class: compile-time via method overloading (three deposit methods with different parameters — the compiler chooses the correct one based on arguments) and runtime via Object inheritance (overriding toString, equals, and hashCode — when called through an Object reference, the JVM dispatches to the BankAccount version at runtime).

In my BankAccount class, `deposit(5000)`, `deposit(5000, "Salary")`, and `deposit(5000, "Salary", "NEFT-REF")` are three overloaded methods — compile-time polymorphism. `account.toString()` returns "SAV2001 (Rajesh): Rs.125000" instead of Object's default "BankAccount@1a2b3c" — this is runtime polymorphism because the JVM dispatches to the overridden method based on the actual object type. HashSet correctly deduplicates accounts by accountId because equals and hashCode are overridden from Object — proving both inheritance and polymorphism.

This is a tricky interview question designed to test DEPTH of OOP understanding. Most candidates give examples with parent-child class hierarchies — but OOP is baked into Java itself. Every class inherits from Object. Every private field is encapsulation. Every public-method-hiding-private-logic is abstraction. Every overloaded method is compile-time polymorphism. The four pillars are not just design patterns you apply — they are fundamental properties of every Java class.
